newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Louthean on Australian Mining - Emerging Mongolia.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Louthean on Australian Mining - Emerging Mongolia.

text.p: *By Ross Louthean
What do Western Australia, Mongolia and an extrovert French-Canadian prospector have in common?

All are now interested in Mongolia, one of the poorest tourist spots in the world but seen -- after the collapse of the Soviet empire -- as the new emerging country for resource development, particularly gold.

Armand Beaudoin, one of the strode venturers of global prospecting, has taken a shine to Mongolia to the point that his company Golden Tiger Corp now employs 140 locals, is gearing up a mining operation, striking joint ventures and has applied for prospects throughout this landlocked country, including near the Gobi Desert.

Beaudoin is in Western Australia this week with a delegation of 10 Mongolian Government officials and geologists keen to see resource development. Premier Richard Court took time off the election campaign to give them a pep talk about how to develop.

The French-Canadian, who had spent 16 years in Australia, was convinced that the Mongolians should see Western Australia not only as a place with desert, dry and remote areas to develop major mines, but also as a role model for mining legislation and having the structure to lure exploreers and development capital.

Beaudoin told me that Richard Court had pointed out that Western Australia was a Cinderella with mineral development until it set up ground rules and incentives to open up remote areas and create mining infrastructure for long term mines.

No doubt the premier had in the back of his mind his father, Sir Charles Court, who as Minister for Resource Development and later premier, helped engineer the legislation and deals for projects such as the Pilbara iron ore mines from the 1960s.
CONFERENCE SEEN CURTAIN RAISER TO LURE EXPLORERS

The prospector said Court showed great enthusiasm and indicated the government would be keen to attend a conference in the Mongolian capital Ulan Bator in June which is seen by Beaudoin as a curtain raiser to luring explorers to Mongolia.

The prospector hopes existing requirements such as high taxation and a 10 percent royalty should be dispensed, particularly as Premier Court had indicated there was no state royalty on gold production in Western Australia (though some of his party are pushing for one should the Liberal-Nationals coalition be re-elected).

The Mongolian delegation, before going to Kalgoorlie to see how an isolated mining centre can thrive, spent some time with the Western Australia Mines Department and took a keen interest in the department's Tengraph computer system which logs WA mineral tenements, their regional positioning and to generally administer the logging and relinquishing of licences.
Mongolia, bereft of capital and having no mining law and accurate system to delineate and manage mining tenements, thanks to the Russians, needs something like Tengraph.
The delegation has told Western Australia mining industry people that they expect to have attractive mining legislation in place before the Ulan Bator conference.
Beaudoin agrees that Mongolia, now desperate for foreign capital and projects to create jobs, will use the guidance of the International Finance Committee.
WESTERN AUSTRALIA SEEN INSPIRATION

He sees WA as a great support because of the entrepreneurial spirit of its exploration and mining community but also because it houses great engineering and technical skills and an access route for materials he believes is not too complex.

Placer gold operations are the current prime source of mining income and while the scope can be broadened by modern exploration -- including aeromagnetic surveys, the likes of which have opened up desert areas of Australia like the Tanami Desert of Western Australia and the northern Territory and the Gawler Craton of South Australia.

But even with Today's operations Beaudoin is exasperated by the legacy of antiquated Russian mining applicaions, where material seen as overburden is stripped to mine narrow channels of placer gold, generally grading 2 grams/tonne. This overburden actually contains lower grade gold and generally fine material that the Mongols have found hard to recover.

So, bulk mining methods similar to those used in Western Australia open cut gold mines is seen as the answer, and Beaudoin's company Golden Tiger Corporation is creanking up bucketwheel excavators and mobile recovery plants in Mongolia's Zaamar goldfield.

A thorough study of Mongolia's gold potential was produced recently by prominent British mining consultant Richard Sillitoe and a group of Mongolian geoscientists and published by Mining Magazine, put out by the London-based Mining Journal group.
This report said placer gold was mined in Mongolia before the Eurasian reign of Ghengis Khan.
SEARCH IN ITS INFANCY

But, unlike Beaudoin, Sillitoe believes logging of the geology and known mineral deposits has been 'comprehensive' but he agrees the quest for hard rock gold ore, particularly as a source of the placer material, as in its infancy.
However, about 400 occurrences were outlined as having scope for potential vein gold and other mineralisation, including porphyry copper-gold targets.

Beaudoin stole a march on the new wave of international explorers now crawling around the jungles of Indonesia, for he left Australia -- after working years before in the Arctic Circle, elsewhere in Canada and South America -- in 1985.

His Golden Tiger has a series of joint ventures for gold and base metals throughout Indonesia. Partners include Highlands Gold Ltd, Robert Friedland's Indochina Goldfields Ltd, Phelps Dodge Corp, Coolgardie gold miner Herald Resources Ltd, Canada's Yamana Resources and New Zealand alluvial gold miner L & M Mining Ltd, owned by DML Resources Ltd which is now changing hands.
He will be remembered by many Australian miners as outraging the conventional mining wisdom by suggesting he had discovered near the famous Fimiston leases another 'hidden Golden Mile'.
Those were the days when deep gold deposits around Kalgoorlie were essentially considered confined to Fimiston and Mt Charlotte.
Armand never hung around to prove his theory but there are many other mines around Kalgoorlie to show how profound the gold mineralisation is at the Western Australian gold capital.
* Ross Louthean is editor of Paydirt and publisher of Gold Mining Journal, The Australian Mines Handbook and Mineral Resources of New Zealand.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
